# Results {#sec-results}

## The problem with current visualisations {#sec-pie-chart-problem}

Before turning to this thesis's main results, it is worth demonstrating directly why mosaic plots -- rather than the pie charts (or equivalent bar charts) that commonly accompany a sample or panel's reported composition in current sortition practice -- are used throughout this chapter, rather than simply asserting it (@sec-methodology).

```{r}
#| label: fig-pie-chart-problem
#| fig-cap: "Pie charts displaying age (left column) and tenure (right column) marginal proportions for the independent population (top) and associated population (bottom). The age categories range from 15%-25% and roughly half of the population owns their home. Notably, these marginal distributions are exactly the same, which hides any association."
#| fig-alt: "Four pie charts in a two-by-two grid: age proportions and tenure proportions for the independent population on top, and for the associated population on the bottom. The age and tenure pie charts look visually identical between the two populations despite one population having an underlying age-tenure association."
#| out-width: "70%"
invisible(capture.output(source("scripts/pie_chart_problem_thesis.R")))

pie_chart_patchwork
```

@fig-pie-chart-problem uses this thesis's own independent and associated populations (`sim_data2`, `sim_data2_cov`) to make the point concrete: the raking procedure used to build the associated population restores the independent population's marginals while retaining the age-renting association introduced beforehand (@sec-methodology), so the largest gap between the two populations' marginal proportions, across any single age bracket or tenure category, is only `{r} round(max(age_marginal_gap, tenure_marginal_gap), 2)` percentage points -- attributable to sampling noise alone.

Yet the two populations are not the same: the associated population carries a genuine, and statistically detectable (@tbl-association-summary-2var), negative association between age and renting, while the independent population has none at all. A pie chart -- or a bar chart, which encodes exactly the same single-variable information in a different shape -- has no visual channel available to show this: it can only display one categorical variable's marginal distribution at a time, so two variables each need their own, entirely separate chart, and nothing in either chart can reveal how the two co-occur. A practitioner shown only the pie charts in @fig-pie-chart-problem would have no way of telling the independent and associated populations apart, despite one holding a materially different -- and, as @sec-panel-association-results goes on to show, selection-relevant -- relationship between age and tenure than the other. The mosaic plots used throughout the remainder of this chapter (@sec-methodology) exist specifically to close this gap, representing both variables' marginal distributions and their joint, intersectional distribution within a single figure.

## Simulation visualisations

### Simulation pipeline: population, slice and respondents (equal-chance case)

```{r}
#| label: fig-pop1-pipeline-eq
#| fig-cap: "Mosaic plots tracing the independent population's age-tenure structure across the population (left panel), a random 10,000-person slice (middle panel), and the slice's respondents under equal-chance response (right panel). Age brackets sit on the x-axis and tenure as fill throughout. Notice that the tile pattern barely shifts from population to respondents -- there is no association between age and tenure to begin with, so neither slicing nor equal-chance response introduces one."
#| fig-alt: "Three mosaic plots side by side, each with age brackets on the x-axis and tenure as colour fill, for the independent population, a 10,000-person slice, and equal-chance respondents. Tenure fill proportions stay level across every age bar in all three plots, showing no age-tenure association at any stage."
#| out-width: "90%"
# source() only suppresses console output for print.eval-gated
# top-level expressions; the sourced scripts' str() calls write
# directly to the console regardless, so capture.output() is used to
# discard everything they print, leaving only the patchwork objects
# (pop1_pipeline_eq, pop2_pipeline_eq) to render below.
invisible(capture.output(source("scripts/patchwork.R")))

pop1_pipeline_eq
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pop2-pipeline-eq
#| fig-cap: "Mosaic plots tracing the associated population's age-tenure structure across the population (left panel), a random 10,000-person slice (middle panel), and the slice's respondents under equal-chance response (right panel). Renting narrows steadily with age, from around 44% among 18-34 year olds to around 18% among those 65 and over. Importantly, this negative age-renting association survives essentially unchanged from population to slice to respondents, confirming equal-chance response doesn't disturb it."
#| fig-alt: "Three mosaic plots side by side, each with age brackets on the x-axis and tenure as colour fill, for the associated population, a 10,000-person slice, and equal-chance respondents. The renting segment shrinks steadily from the youngest to the oldest age bar in all three plots."
#| out-width: "90%"
invisible(capture.output(source("scripts/patchwork.R")))

pop2_pipeline_eq
```

@fig-pop1-pipeline-eq and @fig-pop2-pipeline-eq trace each population's age-tenure structure across the three pipeline stages under the equal-chance response case. Both populations skew towards upper-middle age and a higher frequency of homeownership than other categories. As the captions show, each population's age-tenure relationship (or lack of one) carries through essentially unchanged across all three stages, confirming that neither random slicing nor equal-chance response meaningfully disturbs either population's underlying structure.

### Simulation pipeline: population, slice and respondents (age-associated case)

```{r}
#| label: fig-pop1-pipeline-ass
#| fig-cap: "Mosaic plots tracing the independent population's age-tenure structure across the population (left panel), a random 10,000-person slice (middle panel), and the slice's respondents under age-associated response (right panel), where response likelihood rises from around 20% among 18-34 year olds to over 50% among those 65 and over. Even though age and tenure carry no association in this population, the older age brackets visibly widen among respondents -- differential response alone reshapes who appears, independent of any trait association in the underlying population."
#| fig-alt: "Three mosaic plots side by side for the independent population, a 10,000-person slice, and age-associated respondents. The older age bars widen and younger age bars narrow between the slice and respondents plots, while tenure fill proportions stay level within each bar throughout."
#| out-width: "90%"
# source() only suppresses console output for print.eval-gated
# top-level expressions; the sourced scripts' str() calls write
# directly to the console regardless, so capture.output() is used to
# discard everything they print, leaving only the patchwork objects
# (pop1_pipeline_ass, pop2_pipeline_ass) to render below.
invisible(capture.output(source("scripts/patchwork.R")))

pop1_pipeline_ass
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pop2-pipeline-ass
#| fig-cap: "Mosaic plots tracing the associated population's age-tenure structure across the population (left panel), a random 10,000-person slice (middle panel), and the slice's respondents under age-associated response (right panel). Here, the age skew from differential response compounds with the population's existing negative age-renting association rather than replacing it -- respondents end up weighted even further toward the older, lower-renting end of the distribution than the slice or population alone."
#| fig-alt: "Three mosaic plots side by side for the associated population, a 10,000-person slice, and age-associated respondents. The renting segment shrinks with age in all three plots, and the older age bars widen further between the slice and respondents plots."
#| out-width: "90%"
invisible(capture.output(source("scripts/patchwork.R")))

pop2_pipeline_ass
```

@fig-pop1-pipeline-ass and @fig-pop2-pipeline-ass repeat the same three-stage pipeline, but with response likelihood now rising with age rather than being equal across brackets. Unlike the equal-chance case, the age-tenure structure is no longer preserved unchanged once respondents are reached, as the captions show: an association between age and response probability -- entirely independent of any association between age and tenure in the underlying population -- is sufficient on its own to shift the overall age composition, and therefore the intersections present, in the final respondent sample, compounding with rather than replacing any existing age-tenure relationship in the population it is drawn from.

### Quantifying association across the pipeline

The mosaic patchworks above show the age-tenure association visually; @tbl-association-summary-2var quantifies it at every stage, using a chi-squared test of independence and Cramer's V as an effect-size measure of how strong that association is.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-association-summary-2var
#| tbl-cap: "Chi-squared test of independence and Cramer's V for the age-tenure association at each stage of the two-variable pipeline, for both populations and both response cases. The independent population never reaches significance at any stage (Cramer's V below 0.03 throughout), while the associated population is significant at every stage, with Cramer's V holding steady between roughly 0.125 and 0.132."
#| results: asis
invisible(capture.output(source("scripts/association_summary.R")))

if (knitr::is_latex_output()) cat("\\footnotesize\n")

knitr::kable(
  association_summary_2var[, c(
    "population", "case", "stage", "n", "chi_sq", "df", "p_value_fmt", "cramers_v"
  )],
  col.names = c(
    "Population", "Response case", "Stage", "n", "Chi-sq", "df", "p-value", "Cramer's V"
  ),
  digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 3),
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r")
)

if (knitr::is_latex_output()) cat("\n\\normalsize")
```

@tbl-association-summary-2var confirms what @fig-pop1-pipeline-eq through @fig-pop2-pipeline-ass show visually: an age-tenure association that is genuinely absent in the independent population, not merely undetected, and one that is neither diluted by slicing nor meaningfully inflated by either response case in the associated population -- the age-associated case's effect shows up mainly as a shift in the respondents' age *composition* (@fig-pop1-pipeline-ass, @fig-pop2-pipeline-ass), not as a change in the strength of the age-tenure relationship itself. One caveat applies to the independent population's $p$-values specifically: with population and slice sample sizes in the tens of thousands, even this chi-squared test has the power to detect very small deviations from independence, so the consistently non-significant results here reflect a genuine absence of association, not a lack of statistical power.

## Panel-level association evaluation {#sec-panel-association-results}

### Overview across lottery files

```{r}
#| label: load-panel-association-results
#| include: false
# performance_evaluator.R sources scripts/lottery_helpers.R, which in
# turn sources scripts/simdata2.R; capture.output() discards that
# chain's console output (str(), chisq.test() printouts, etc.),
# leaving lottery_summary and lottery_evaluations available below.
invisible(capture.output(source("scripts/performance_evaluator.R")))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-panel-association-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Panel-level association results across all four lottery files: survey-sample-level age-tenure association, and the proportion of possible panels whose association was found to be significantly different from the sample's. The proportion flagged as significantly different is saturated at or near 100% across all four files, regardless of whether the underlying population carries a genuine age-tenure association or none at all."
#| results: asis
# Display order follows increasing association (ind_eq, ind_ass,
# cov_eq, cov_ass), matching @tbl-association-summary-2var, rather
# than the alphabetical order lottery_summary is built in.
file_order <- c(
  "lottery_ind_eq.csv", "lottery_ind_ass.csv",
  "lottery_cov_eq.csv", "lottery_cov_ass.csv"
)

if (knitr::is_latex_output()) cat("\\footnotesize\n")

knitr::kable(
  lottery_summary[order(match(lottery_summary$file, file_order)), c(
    "file", "n_panels", "sample_association_p", "sample_cramers_v", "prop_sig_different"
  )],
  col.names = c(
    "Lottery file", "Panels", "Sample assoc. p", "Sample Cramer's V",
    "Prop. significantly different"
  ),
  digits = c(0, 0, 3, 3, 3),
  row.names = FALSE
)

if (knitr::is_latex_output()) cat("\n\\normalsize")
```

@tbl-panel-association-summary summarises the results across all four lottery files. In the associated population, the survey sample itself retains a clearly detectable age-tenure association (Cramer's V around `{r} round(mean(lottery_summary$sample_cramers_v[grepl("cov", lottery_summary$file)]), 2)`), consistent with the negative age-renting relationship built into the population design. In the independent population, by contrast, the sample-level association is negligible and statistically indistinguishable from zero (both $p > 0.5$), exactly as expected given no association was introduced between age and tenure at the population level.

Despite this contrast in the underlying samples, the proportion of panels flagged as holding a significantly different association from their sample is strikingly similar -- and strikingly high -- across all four files: between `{r} round(min(lottery_summary$prop_sig_different) * 100, 1)`% and `{r} round(max(lottery_summary$prop_sig_different) * 100, 1)`%. In other words, essentially every panel Panelot could possibly return, under either population structure and either response-rate case, exhibits an age-tenure relationship detectably different from the sample it was drawn from -- including in the independent population, where there is no true association for a panel to even distort.

Splitting this range apart by file shows little further structure: the two equal-chance lotteries (`lottery_cov_eq.csv`, `lottery_ind_eq.csv`) each flag 100% of their feasible panels, while the two age-associated lotteries fall only fractionally short, at `{r} round(lottery_summary$prop_sig_different[lottery_summary$file == "lottery_cov_ass.csv"] * 100, 2)`% and `{r} round(lottery_summary$prop_sig_different[lottery_summary$file == "lottery_ind_ass.csv"] * 100, 2)`% respectively -- despite these two files containing roughly twice as many feasible panels (`{r} lottery_summary$n_panels[lottery_summary$file == "lottery_cov_ass.csv"]` and `{r} lottery_summary$n_panels[lottery_summary$file == "lottery_ind_ass.csv"]`, against `{r} lottery_summary$n_panels[lottery_summary$file == "lottery_cov_eq.csv"]` and `{r} lottery_summary$n_panels[lottery_summary$file == "lottery_ind_eq.csv"]`), and therefore more opportunities for an occasional panel to be drawn that does not diverge from its sample. Neither population structure nor response case moves the result in a way that a difference of a few feasible panels out of several thousand cannot already explain -- the distortion identified here looks like a property of the quota mechanism itself, not of any particular population or response structure it happens to be applied to.

This saturation pattern also speaks to a design concern about the panel-versus-sample test raised in @sec-panel-association-methods: because Panelot's quota constraints are set from each category's *population* marginal distribution rather than the survey sample's own marginals, a panel could in principle diverge from its sample simply because the sample's composition has drifted from the population's, rather than because of anything specific to the selection mechanism. Under equal-chance response, however, the survey sample's age marginal already matches the population's closely (@fig-pop1-pipeline-eq, @fig-pop2-pipeline-eq), leaving barely any population-versus-sample gap for population-based quotas to correct -- yet the equal-chance files above are flagged as different *at least as often* as the age-associated ones, where the sample's marginal has genuinely drifted from the population's (@fig-pop1-pipeline-ass, @fig-pop2-pipeline-ass). If population correction were driving the divergence, equal-chance panels should have been flagged less often, not equally or more. Together with the test's own design -- which already allows panel and sample to differ freely on each marginal without that alone counting as significant (@sec-panel-association-methods) -- this confirms that the near-total divergence documented here reflects the quota mechanism leaving the joint age-tenure distribution unconstrained, rather than any population-versus-sample drift.

### Comparison against the random-sampling benchmark

```{r}
#| label: srs-benchmark
#| include: false
set.seed(6821)

n_reps <- 500
file_keys <- c(cov_eq = "cov_eq", cov_ass = "cov_ass", ind_eq = "ind_eq", ind_ass = "ind_ass")

srs_benchmark_for <- function(key) {
  pool <- survey_samples[[key]]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_reps), function(r) {
    ids <- sample(pool$ID, 50)
    members <- pool[pool$ID %in% ids, ]
    within <- test_within_panel(members)
    vs_p <- test_panel_vs_sample(ids, pool)
    data.frame(cramers_v = within$cramers_v, vs_sample_p = vs_p)
  }))
}

srs_results <- lapply(file_keys, srs_benchmark_for)

benchmark_comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(file_keys), function(key) {
  lottery_file <- paste0("lottery_", key, ".csv")
  panels <- lottery_evaluations[[lottery_file]]$results
  srs_df <- srs_results[[key]]
  data.frame(
    lottery_file = lottery_file,
    n_panels = nrow(panels),
    prop_sig_panels = mean(panels$sig_different),
    median_cramers_v_panels = median(panels$within_panel_cramers_v),
    # A handful of 50-member random draws land on a zero marginal
    # (e.g. no 18-34 renters), for which Cramer's V is undefined;
    # these are excluded from the SRS median rather than the panel
    # one, since panels are quota-constrained and never produce a
    # zero marginal.
    prop_sig_srs = mean(srs_df$vs_sample_p < 0.05),
    median_cramers_v_srs = median(srs_df$cramers_v, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-srs-benchmark
#| tbl-cap: "Proportion of panels (or random samples) whose age-tenure association was found to be significantly different from the survey sample's, and the median within-group Cramer's V, for actual sortition panels versus 500 simple random samples of equal size, for all four lottery files. Sortition panels are flagged as different an order of magnitude more often than equivalently sized random samples, with roughly three times the median Cramer's V."
#| results: asis
# benchmark_comparison$lottery_file carries the full "lottery_*.csv"
# name; displaying just the "<ind|cov>_<eq|ass>" key (already
# introduced as this file-naming convention earlier in the chapter),
# alongside shorter column headers, keeps all six columns narrow
# enough that the "Lottery file" and "Panels" columns no longer
# collide once rendered at full page width.
benchmark_display <- benchmark_comparison
benchmark_display$lottery_file <- gsub(
  "^lottery_|\\.csv$", "", benchmark_display$lottery_file
)

if (knitr::is_latex_output()) cat("\\footnotesize\n")

knitr::kable(
  benchmark_display,
  col.names = c(
    "Lottery file", "Panels", "Prop. sig. diff. (panels)", "Median V (panels)",
    "Prop. sig. diff. (SRS)", "Median V (SRS)"
  ),
  digits = c(0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 3),
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r")
)

if (knitr::is_latex_output()) cat("\n\\normalsize")
```

@tbl-srs-benchmark repeats the comparison introduced in @sec-panel-association-methods across all four lottery files, rather than the single associated/equal-chance case alone. Actual sortition panels are flagged as significantly different from their sample `{r} round(min(benchmark_comparison$prop_sig_panels) * 100, 1)`-100% of the time, against only `{r} round(min(benchmark_comparison$prop_sig_srs) * 100, 1)`-`{r} round(max(benchmark_comparison$prop_sig_srs) * 100, 1)`% for equivalently sized random samples -- modestly above the nominal 5% false-positive rate expected under the null (plausibly the homogeneity test's asymptotic approximation being somewhat liberal at this cell count, rather than genuine divergence from random sampling). Median within-group Cramer's V tells the same story: panels sit around `{r} round(min(benchmark_comparison$median_cramers_v_panels), 2)`-`{r} round(max(benchmark_comparison$median_cramers_v_panels), 2)`, against `{r} round(min(benchmark_comparison$median_cramers_v_srs), 2)`-`{r} round(max(benchmark_comparison$median_cramers_v_srs), 2)` seen from random draws, in every file regardless of population or response case. Because the benchmark result holds uniformly, rather than being specific to the associated/equal-chance file used as the illustrative case above, the explanation cannot be population- or response-case-specific either -- reinforcing that it is Panelot's quota mechanism, not sampling variability at panel size or any one simulated condition, driving the divergence documented in @tbl-panel-association-summary.

```{r}
#| label: load-panel-visualiser
#| include: false
invisible(capture.output(source("scripts/panel_visualiser.R")))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-panel-vs-sample-example
#| fig-cap: "Age-tenure composition of the associated population's survey sample (left) alongside its most likely panel under lottery_cov_eq.csv (right). Although the panel satisfies the same marginal age and tenure quotas as the sample, its age-tenure combinations are considerably more blocky and uneven -- several age brackets end up filled by entirely one tenure category, exaggerating the sample's already-present age-renting association."
#| fig-alt: "Two mosaic plots side by side comparing age-tenure composition: the survey sample on the left shows a smooth gradient in the renting segment across age brackets, while the selected panel on the right shows a blockier pattern with several age brackets almost entirely one tenure category."
#| out-width: "68%"
plot_panel_vs_sample(cov_eq_source, most_likely_panel_id)
```

@fig-panel-vs-sample-example makes explicit what the aggregate figures above describe in summary: the smooth, gradually strengthening sample-level relationship between age and renting gives way to a considerably more extreme, blocky panel-level pattern, despite the panel satisfying the same marginal quotas as the sample it was ostensibly drawn to represent.

```{r}
#| label: fig-panel-vs-sample-independent
#| fig-cap: "Age-tenure composition of the independent population's survey sample (left) alongside its most likely panel under lottery_ind_eq.csv (right). Even though age and tenure carry no association in the sample -- its fill proportions sit close to flat across every age bracket -- the panel still ends up blocky and uneven, with most age brackets dominated by a single tenure category, showing the distortion is an artefact of selection itself rather than an exaggeration of a real trend."
#| fig-alt: "Two mosaic plots side by side comparing age-tenure composition for the independent population: the survey sample on the left shows flat tile heights across all age brackets, while the selected panel on the right shows an uneven, blocky pattern with most age brackets dominated by a single tenure category."
#| out-width: "68%"
ind_eq_source <- load_panel_source(file.path(lottery_dir, "lottery_ind_eq.csv"))
most_likely_ind_eq <- which.max(ind_eq_source$lottery$return_probability)

plot_panel_vs_sample(ind_eq_source, most_likely_ind_eq)
```

@fig-panel-vs-sample-independent shows the same comparison for the independent population. The panel is, if anything, more extreme than the associated-population example: the within-panel test gives a Cramer's V of `{r} round(test_within_panel(get_panel_members(ind_eq_source, most_likely_ind_eq))$cramers_v, 2)`, versus `{r} round(lottery_summary$sample_cramers_v[lottery_summary$file == "lottery_ind_eq.csv"], 2)` for the sample it was drawn from. Because this panel's distorted joint structure cannot be attributed to a genuine association it is "exaggerating" -- there is none to exaggerate in the independent population -- it most directly demonstrates that the within-panel association test is picking up an artefact of the selection mechanism, not a real signal faithfully (if imperfectly) carried through from the sample.

### Summary

Across all four simulated conditions, satisfying Panelot's marginal quotas on age and tenure did not translate into a panel whose joint age-tenure structure resembled its survey sample's: essentially every feasible panel was flagged as significantly different from the sample, at a rate far beyond what panel size alone could explain, and this held regardless of whether the underlying population carried a genuine age-tenure association or response was skewed by age. Marginal quota satisfaction -- the only form of representativeness that a current sortition tool like Panelot reports to a practitioner -- is therefore not a reliable proxy for intersectional representativeness in this simulation, and the gap between the two looks like a structural consequence of leaving the joint distribution unconstrained, rather than an artefact of this thesis's particular panel size or association strengths. This divergence is not attributable to panels merely correcting toward population marginals where the sample itself has drifted -- a possibility already ruled out above, both by the panel-versus-sample test's design and by the data (@sec-panel-association-results; @sec-methodology). @sec-application introduces Intersection Inspector, a tool built directly in response to this marginal-versus-intersectional gap, which displays a panel's intersectional association alongside its marginal quota satisfaction so that this kind of distortion is visible to a practitioner before a panel convenes, rather than only to a reader of this thesis after the fact.
